titre: Elisha Otis Didn't Invent the Elevator, Just the Brake That Made It Safe
accroche: In 1852, in a Yonkers bedstead factory, Elisha Otis invents a brake that locks a hoist if the rope breaks. Without that lock, no skyscraper.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1852, Elisha Otis works as a mechanic at the Maize & Burns bedstead factory in Yonkers, New York. The plant needs to lift heavy machinery to an upper floor using a hoist suspended by a single rope, and a rope that breaks drops the platform with nothing to stop it. Otis isn't trying to invent the elevator: hoists and lifts have existed since antiquity, powered by hand, water, or steam. He's only trying to keep his from killing someone.

## A Ratchet That Only Works When the Rope Fails

Otis's device rests on a platform that slides between two vertical, toothed guide rails. As long as the rope pulls the platform upward, a system of rods and levers keeps two pawls away from the teeth, so they don't slow the climb. The moment the rope's tension disappears, whether it breaks, comes loose, or goes slack, the levers release the pawls, which immediately catch in the rails' teeth and lock the platform in place. The report published by Scientific American on November 25, 1854, describes this mechanism piece by piece, diagram included: if the rope should fail, the magazine writes, the platform "will be sustained" and "prevented from falling."

In 1854, Otis demonstrates his brake at the World's Fair in New York, inside the Crystal Palace: he stands on a platform hoisted high up and has the supporting rope cut. The platform drops only a few inches before the pawls catch it. The exact date and the details of the stunt vary across accounts, but the commercial effect is clear: orders, until then rare, multiply. Otis leaves the bedstead factory to found his own company.

## A Bet Placed Before the Invention

On March 23, 1857, Otis installs the first passenger safety elevator, at 488 Broadway, in Eder V. Haughwout's china shop. Four years earlier already, in 1853, industrialist Peter Cooper had built a round elevator shaft in his new institute in New York, betting that a safe elevator would soon be invented: the architecture anticipated the technology before it even existed.

## What This Brake Shifts

Otis invented nothing that moves people: he only made vertical transport trustworthy. Yet it's this lock, not the hoist itself, that lets an office building rise past the five or six floors a visitor will still climb on foot. The first office building designed around the passenger elevator, the Equitable Life Building in New York, opens in 1870, thirteen years after the installation at Haughwout's. Historians of technology have since noted that the Crystal Palace legend, repeated in nearly every account of elevator history, has likely grown more dramatic thanks to the later success of the Otis Elevator Company: the machine that changed the shape of cities isn't the car, but the device that keeps it from falling.

repere.texte: On March 23, 1857, the first passenger safety elevator enters service at 488 Broadway, New York, in Eder V. Haughwout's store. The Equitable Life Building, the first office building designed around the passenger elevator, wouldn't open until thirteen years later, in 1870.

carte.punch: Otis didn't invent the elevator: he invented the brake that made it safe.
carte.idee: In 1852, Elisha Otis invents a ratchet that locks a hoist if the rope breaks. Demonstrated at New York's Crystal Palace in 1854, this brake makes the passenger elevator credible: without it, office buildings don't rise past five or six floors.

quiz.question: What did Elisha Otis actually invent in 1852?
choix: The first hoist powered by a rope
A ratchet brake that automatically locks the platform if the rope fails
The enclosed metal cab, replacing the open platform
quiz.explication: Hoists already existed, powered by hand, water, or steam. Otis's invention is the safety device: pawls that catch in toothed guide rails the moment the rope's tension disappears, locking the platform before it can fall.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did industrialist Peter Cooper build in 1853, even before Otis's demonstration?
choix: A hydraulic elevator powered by rainwater
A round elevator shaft in his new institute, betting that a safe elevator would soon be invented
A prototype toothed ratchet, later sold to Otis
The first office building fully served by an elevator
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cooper built the shaft before a safe elevator even existed, anticipating the invention. The toothed ratchet is Otis's, not Cooper's, and the first office building served this way is the Equitable Life Building, in 1870.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when does Otis's first passenger safety elevator enter service?
choix: The Maize & Burns factory, in Yonkers, in 1852
The World's Fair in New York, in 1854
The Equitable Life Building, New York, in 1870
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1852 factory is where Otis invents his brake, the 1854 demonstration took place at the Crystal Palace, and the 1870 Equitable Life Building is the first office building built around the elevator, thirteen years later, not the first elevator installed.
